note: WebFetch returned 403 for ohchr.org, so OHCHR and treaties.un.org pages were opened with curl and a browser User-Agent. Several Wikipedia case pages returned 404 and those claims are marked unverifiable. Written in one final pass after all sources were checked. Topics from 2024 to 2026 that the lessons leave out: KlimaSeniorinnen v Switzerland (ECtHR GC, April 2024) is not mentioned. The Council of Europe and ECHR migration-interpretation debate (2025-26) is not mentioned. The US left the Human Rights Council (Feb 2025) and skipped its UPR (Nov 2025). Hungary's Rome Statute withdrawal took effect 2 June 2026, and Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger gave notice in June 2026. Tunisia withdrew its Art 34(6) declaration in March 2025. The EU CSDDD was cut back by Omnibus I. None of these makes a lesson sentence false, except the CSDDD hedge in l16, which is now stale. No option text is cut off mid-sentence. Typo: l17.q5 says 'Which of these states is correct' where 'statements' is meant.

questions.note: A signatory still has the VCLT Art 18 duty not to defeat the treaty's object and purpose, so 'does not bind as treaty law' is slightly simplified, but choice 3 is clearly the best.
Correct in design, but the US refused to take part in its November 2025 UPR (the review was rescheduled to 2026), so 'covers every UN member' now has a live exception.
Roper concerns only the death penalty. The closer US authority on juvenile life without parole is Graham v Florida (2010) or Miller v Alabama (2012). Choice 1 is still the only defensible answer.
The OPAC sets 18 for compulsory recruitment and requires 'all feasible measures' against direct participation under 18. Voluntary recruitment may start at 16.
Under Jesner, a foreign corporate defendant would also be dismissed on that separate ground.
Prompt typo: 'Which of these states is correct' should read 'statements'.

claims.claim: UDHR adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948 as resolution 217A (III), 48 votes to 0 with 8 abstentions.
The abstainers included the Soviet bloc states, South Africa and Saudi Arabia.
claims.note: Six communist states, Saudi Arabia and South Africa. Honduras and Yemen did not vote.

claims.claim: UN Charter Articles 1(3), 55 and 56 make promotion of human rights a purpose and a pledge, without listing rights.
claims.note: Matches my understanding, but I did not open the Charter text.

claims.claim: ICCPR and ICESCR adopted 16 December 1966 and in force in 1976.
claims.note: ICCPR in force 23 Mar 1976 (175 parties) and ICESCR 3 Jan 1976 (174 parties), per UNTC status at 2 Oct 2026.

claims.claim: The US ratified the ICCPR in 1992 and signed but never ratified the ICESCR; China signed the ICCPR in 1998 without ratifying, and ratified the ICESCR.
claims.note: US: ICCPR ratified 8 Jun 1992, ICESCR signed 5 Oct 1977. China: ICCPR signed 5 Oct 1998, ICESCR ratified 27 Mar 2001.

claims.claim: The Optional Protocol to the ICESCR was adopted in 2008 and in force since 2013.
claims.note: Adopted 10 Dec 2008, in force 5 May 2013.

claims.claim: The Human Rights Council was created in 2006 and has 47 member states elected by the General Assembly.
claims.note: The page confirms 2006 and 47 members. It does not show resolution 60/251 itself.

claims.claim: In the UPR every UN member has its human rights record reviewed in turn.
claims.note: True in design, but the US (which disengaged from the HRC by executive order in Feb 2025) refused to take part in its Nov 2025 review, which was rescheduled to 2026. Worth a currency note.

claims.claim: CESCR was established by ECOSOC in 1985 rather than by the Covenant; the ICJ in Diallo (2010) gave great weight to Human Rights Committee interpretation.
claims.note: The ICJ page confirms the Diallo merits judgment of 30 Nov 2010 and the ICCPR violations found, but not the 'great weight' wording. The OHCHR CESCR page confirms 18 experts but not the 1985 ECOSOC origin.

claims.claim: The ICJ's 1951 advisory opinion on Reservations to the Genocide Convention adopted the object-and-purpose test.
claims.note: Advisory Opinion of 28 May 1951.

claims.claim: General Comment 24 (1994): the Committee assesses compatibility, and incompatible reservations are severable.
claims.note: Adopted 2 Nov 1994.

claims.claim: Belgium v Senegal (2012) recognised CAT obligations as erga omnes partes; DRC v Rwanda (2006) held that peremptory status did not create jurisdiction; Barcelona Traction (1970).
claims.note: Judgments of 20 Jul 2012, 3 Feb 2006 and 5 Feb 1970.

claims.claim: Grootboom (South African Constitutional Court, 2000): the housing programme was unreasonable for making no provision for people in desperate need.
claims.note: Judgment 4 Oct 2000.

claims.claim: Airey v Ireland (ECtHR, 1979): effective access to court may require legal aid.
claims.note: The year and facts are confirmed. I did not see the 'no water-tight division' wording on the page.

claims.claim: CESCR General Comment 3 (1990) sets out the minimum core and immediate non-discrimination duties.
claims.note: Not checked against an opened page.

claims.claim: A and Others v UK (GC, 2009): an emergency existed, but the measure was disproportionate and discriminatory against non-nationals.
claims.note: Judgment 19 Feb 2009.

claims.claim: ICCPR Art 4(2) non-derogable list: Arts 6, 7, 8(1)-(2), 11, 15, 16, 18.
claims.note: Matches my understanding, but I did not open the treaty text.

claims.claim: Handyside v UK (1976) upheld an obscenity conviction within the margin of appreciation.
claims.note: Not opened.

claims.claim: Protocol 15 in force 2021; the time limit was cut from six to four months from February 2022.
claims.note: In force 1 Aug 2021; four-month limit from 1 Feb 2022.

claims.claim: Russia was expelled in March 2022 and ceased to be a party on 16 September 2022; the Court remains competent for earlier acts.
claims.note: The lesson does not mention the 2025-26 Council of Europe debate on reinterpreting the ECHR on migration, or KlimaSeniorinnen (2024). This is an omission, not an error.

claims.claim: Tyrer v UK (1978): the living-instrument doctrine; birching on the Isle of Man was degrading punishment.
Trinidad and Tobago denounced the American Convention in 1998; Venezuela's denunciation took effect in 2013.
claims.note: T&T notice 26 May 1998 (effective 1999); Venezuela effective 10 Sep 2013.

claims.claim: Velasquez Rodriguez v Honduras (1988) was the Court's first contentious case and set the due-diligence duty to prevent, investigate and punish.
claims.note: Judgment 29 Jul 1988; disappearance in 1981.

claims.claim: Awas Tingni v Nicaragua (2001): Article 21 protects communal customary land without formal title.
claims.note: The Wikipedia page was not found and no other source was opened.

claims.claim: African Charter adopted 1981, in force 1986; Court Protocol adopted 1998, in force 2004, seat in Arusha.
claims.note: Charter 27 Jun 1981 / 21 Oct 1986; Protocol in force 25 Jan 2004.

claims.claim: Only a minority of states made Article 34(6) declarations, and a few have since withdrawn them.
claims.note: Five have withdrawn: Rwanda 2016, Tanzania 2019, Benin and Cote d'Ivoire 2020, Tunisia March 2025. About seven declarations remain.

claims.claim: SERAC v Nigeria (2001), Endorois v Kenya (2009), Ogiek (African Court, 2017); the Arab Charter of 2004 entered into force in 2008 and has a committee but no court.
claims.note: SERAC 27 Oct 2001; Endorois 25 Nov 2009; Ogiek 26 May 2017; Arab Charter in force 15 Mar 2008.

claims.claim: CAT adopted 1984, in force 1987.
claims.note: Adopted 10 Dec 1984, in force 26 Jun 1987, 176 parties.

claims.claim: Ireland v UK (1978): the five techniques were inhuman and degrading but not torture.
Soering (1989), Chahal (1996) and Saadi v Italy (2008) on Article 3 and removal.
claims.note: The years and subjects are confirmed. The holdings match the pages' summaries.

claims.claim: Refugee Convention adopted 1951 (with the 1967 Protocol); Article 33 non-refoulement.
claims.note: Geneva 28 Jul 1951, in force 22 Apr 1954, 146 parties. The lesson does not cover the 2024 EU Pact on Migration and Asylum (applying from June 2026).

claims.claim: INS v Cardoza-Fonseca (1987): well-founded fear is a lower standard than clear probability. Sale v Haitian Centers Council (1993): Article 33 does not restrict high-seas returns.
Hirsi Jamaa v Italy (2012): Italian jurisdiction, an Article 3 breach and a collective expulsion.
claims.note: Grand Chamber judgment 23 Feb 2012.

claims.claim: General Comment 31 (2004): duties extend to anyone within a state's power or effective control.
claims.note: Adopted 29 Mar 2004.

claims.claim: Bankovic (2001) was inadmissible; Al-Skeini (GC 2011) found UK authority and control through its soldiers in Basra.
ILC Articles (2001): Art 4/7 organ conduct even ultra vires; Art 16 aid or assistance with knowledge.
claims.note: Not opened.

claims.claim: CRC adopted 20 Nov 1989, in force 2 Sep 1990; the US signed in 1995 and is the only UN member not to ratify.
claims.note: 196 parties. US signed 16 Feb 1995 and has not ratified.

claims.claim: The communications Optional Protocol was adopted in 2011 and in force from 2014.
claims.note: Adopted 19 Dec 2011, in force 14 Apr 2014.

claims.claim: Roper v Simmons (2005) barred the death penalty for under-18 offenders.
CEDAW adopted 18 Dec 1979, in force 3 Sep 1981; the US signed in 1980 and has not ratified.
claims.note: US signed 17 Jul 1980. 189 parties.

claims.claim: The Optional Protocol was adopted in 1999 and in force from 2000; GR 19 (1992) and GR 35 (2017).
claims.note: OP 6 Oct 1999 / 22 Dec 2000; GR35 adopted 14 Jul 2017.

claims.claim: Opuz v Turkey (2009): violations of Arts 2 and 3 and gender discrimination.
claims.note: 9 Jun 2009; Art 14 with Arts 2 and 3. The lesson cites the Istanbul Convention but does not mention Turkey's 2021 withdrawal from it.

claims.claim: UNDRIP adopted in 2007 by 144-4-11; Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the US voted against and later endorsed it.
Lovelace v Canada (HRC, 1981): exclusion from the reserve violated Article 27.
Saramaka v Suriname (IACtHR, 2007) requires FPIC for large-scale projects.
UNGPs endorsed unanimously by the HRC in 2011 after Ruggie's 2008 Protect, Respect and Remedy framework.
claims.note: HRC resolution 17/4 of 16 Jun 2011.

claims.claim: Vedanta v Lungowe (UKSC 2019) allowed the claim against the parent to proceed; ATS line Kiobel (2013), Jesner (2018), Nestle (2021); Nevsun (SCC 2020).
The EU CSDDD (2024) scope and timeline are 'under political revision' and should be checked.
claims.note: Stale. The revision is finished. Omnibus I was adopted by Parliament on 16 Dec 2025 and is in force from 2026. CSDDD now covers companies with more than 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5bn turnover, with compliance deferred to July 2029.

claims.claim: Pinochet (No 3) (HL 1999): no immunity for torture after 8 December 1988.
Arrest Warrant (ICJ 2002): Belgium violated the immunity of the sitting Congolese foreign minister.
claims.note: Judgment 14 Feb 2002.

claims.claim: In 2019 the ICC Appeals Chamber held that Jordan failed to arrest al-Bashir; the US, China, Russia and India are not parties.
claims.note: 6 May 2019. The non-party list is accurate, but the lesson omits recent withdrawals: Hungary (effective 2 Jun 2026), and Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger (notified June 2026, effective 2027). See https://www.coalitionfortheicc.org/news/hungary-withdraws-icc-rome-statute

claims.claim: The Vienna Declaration (1993): all rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated; particularities must be borne in mind, but states must protect all rights regardless of system.
claims.note: Para 5.

claims.claim: The Cairo Declaration on Human Rights in Islam (1990) of the OIC makes rights subject to Shariah.
claims.note: The page confirms 1990 and the OIC. Shariah subordination is per the page's categories and summary.

claims.claim: The American Anthropological Association statement of 1947 and the Bangkok Declaration of 1993.
claims.note: Not opened.
